LumenWorks to run 100k token mixed workload benchmark and upload logs
Schedule microbench with LumenWorks infra team to test prefix caching on staging (week of 8/25)
SE to attach spike results and cost delta spreadsheet to the CRM record
action_items: Anya - export per-route latency/cost CSV and populate the shared spreadsheet - due 2025-08-22
James - run 100k token benchmark with 10/90 short/long mix and upload results - due 2025-08-26

meeting_header: Date: 2025-08-20 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Anya Kowalski (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (LumenWorks Dir ML), James O'Neill (LumenWorks Eng Mgr), Priya Anand (LumenWorks SRE)
summary: Weekly pilot check-in focused on cost / unit economics. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ and observed caching savings; discussed batching tradeoffs and a plan to run a mixed-workload benchmark. Agreed on updated config share and microbench next week. Action items assigned for CSV export, benchmark runs, and pilot extension paperwork.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call?
[00:06] Marta: Marta here.
[00:08] James: James, hi.
[00:10] Priya: Priya, good afternoon.
[00:12] Anya: Anya from Redwood.
[00:14] Samir: Cool, okay, agenda — we want to go over the cost numbers from last week's runs, discuss the cache impact, and then agree next steps. I'll hand over to Anya for the run recap.
[00:30] Anya: Alright, so I posted the updated sheet, link in the chat — https://redwood.app/sheets/lumenworks-pilot-aug — there are two tabs: mixed-workload and long-only. For the mixed one we measured tokens/sec and normalized dollars using your pilot rate. Quick headline: with prefix caching enabled we saw about a 27% reduction in token spend on the short-turn queries and roughly a 9% improvement in overall tokens/sec because the runtime bypassed repeated prefix compute.
[01:05] James: Wait, 27% on short queries, is that absolute tokens saved or cost after batching?
[01:12] Anya: It's tokens saved from the model runs — so fewer generated tokens because the system reuses K-V cache across the conversation prefixes. The cost reduction is slightly different after batching because batching changes the effective throughput rate; on cost per token it's directly the same but on tokens/sec/$ the batching amortizes overhead so you see combined effects.
[01:41] Marta: Can you remind me the baseline? Which model variant and quantization were we using?
[01:46] Anya: Baseline was redwood-3b-v1-fp16 (we called it r3b-fp16 in the sheet) on a single g520 instance in dedicated mode. We also ran a quantized int8 pass for a smaller bucket of traces; int8 looked like ~1.9x tokens/sec improvement but a slight hit on some long-tail quality checks — we flagged two failure cases in the eval tab.
[02:12] Priya: When you say g520 instance, is that the dedicated pool or the hosted tier we spun up for pilot? I'm trying to map to our infra cost buckets.
[02:20] Samir: This was in your dedicated pilot VPC — the reserved nodes we set aside. The invoice mapping is in the spreadsheet.
[02:26] Priya: Okay got it.
[02:29] James: About batching — you said tokens/sec/$ improved after batching, but latency got worse? Can you quantify?
[02:36] Anya: Sure. We tried three batching configs: conservative (batch size 8, max wait 20ms), aggressive (batch 32, wait 80ms), and adaptive (runtime auto-batching tuned to keep p95 <= 200ms). Conservative had median latency 80ms, p95 220ms, tokens/sec/$ baseline. Aggressive pushed tokens/sec/$ up by ~35% but p95 moved to 420ms which is above your SLO of 300ms. Adaptive hit a sweet spot: tokens/sec/$ +22% and p95 270ms.
[03:09] Marta: That's promising. Our product team's comfortable with p95 up to 300 for async suggestions, but chat UI needs lower. We're splitting routes anyway.
[03:20] James: Right — we can route UI to conservative and background tasks to aggressive. But does adaptive introduce jitter that users will see?
[03:27] Anya: Some jitter yes, but we saw tail smoothing with the adaptive policy because it uses priority weights and per-route routing. It did increase variance for a small fraction of requests — roughly 4% — we flagged those traces.
[03:40] Priya: What about prefix caching durability? Any cache hit rate numbers?
[03:44] Anya: Hit rate on short conversat- — short-turn prefix set was 62% hit rate on staging. That yielded the 27% tokens saved I mentioned. For multi-turn long sessions hit rate drops to ~18% but still helps because KV reuse across contiguous segments reduces compute on the large attention matrices.
[04:06] Samir: Quick note: the cache eviction policy used LRU with a 1.5 GB per-instance cap in pilot; we can tune to MRU or TTL per route if you want different behavior.
[04:16] James: Can you do a scenario where TTL is 30m for session tokens to see if hit rate rises?
[04:20] Anya: Yep, we can run that. I expect hit rate to maybe move to 68-70% for short sessions but cost of memory plus staleness needs to be considered.
[04:32] Marta: Another question on tokens/sec/$ — are these numbers normalized to your hosted pricing or the reserved capacity billing? We need to map to our finance model.
[04:40] Samir: In the sheet we included two columns: pilot effective unit cost (what you're being billed for the pilot) and modeled reserved pricing at scale. The tokens/sec/$ effect is shown for both; the reserved pricing shows better improvements because fixed infra overheads are amortized.
[04:55] James: The reserved model looked attractive but we're nervous about commit size. Can Redwood provide a forecast for committed hours based on our 3-month ramp?
[05:03] Samir: Absolutely, we'll attach a forecast. It's one of the next steps.
[05:07] Priya: On quantization — you mentioned int8 had some quality regressions. How bad were they?
[05:11] Anya: Two failure classes: hallucination in numeric extraction and a slight formatting shift in codegen snippets. They were 0.6% of traces in long-run tests but they occurred in high-sensitivity routes. We recommend using int8 only for background rerank/embeddings-heavy routes, not for UI-sensitive chat until we either patch model or do a hybrid float fallback for certain prompts.
[05:36] Marta: Hybrid fallback sounds interesting — can you explain how that would work?
[05:39] Anya: Sure — route first to quantized int8 model; if quality scores from lightweight evalers fall below threshold, we fallback to fp16 variant for that request. The runtime supports that pattern and Redwood Optimize can autotune thresholds. The cost becomes a weighted average but avoids visible regressions.
[05:59] James: Is that expensive compute-wise? Two model calls maybe double cost on fallback cases?
[06:04] Anya: Fallbacks were rare in our tests (<1.2% of traffic) so overall cost delta was minimal compared to full fp16. But for your high-sensitivity flows we can cap fallback attempts and set stricter thresholds.
[06:20] Priya: I'd like to know the instrumentation needed to run the microbench. What logs do you need from our side?
[06:25] Samir: We asked for request/response traces, per-token latencies, and the route mapping. James, you mentioned you'd capture 100k tokens — can you also include env metadata: instance types, pod contended CPU, and any proxy latency?
[06:38] James: Yep, we'll annotate traces with k8s node and proxy times.
[06:42] Anya: Also include cold-starts vs warm-run flags — the runtime's cold path is slightly higher latency and we want to isolate that.
[06:49] Marta: On caching — will prefix cache work with our ephemeral session IDs? We use rotate tokens per user for privacy.
[06:56] Anya: You can keep session IDs ephemeral but cache on canonicalized prefix (strip session token); Redwood supports canonicalization hooks in the SDK so you can retain privacy while reusing prefixes. We'll share an example snippet.
[07:10] James: Any thoughts on routing between dedicated and hosted for overflow? We had a burst last week and some traffic spilled to the hosted provision.
[07:18] Samir: Smart routing can do regional fallback — we can configure a burst pool in hosted to accept overflow at a slightly higher rate. The runtime supports automated failover with a model variant that is cheaper to run so it's graceful.
[07:31] Priya: Is the overflow audible in billing? How's it tracked?
[07:34] Samir: We log overflow events and show them in the console; billing includes burst usage as separate line items. We'll show how those map to the tokens/sec/$ columns.
[07:45] Marta: Let's talk about the p95 target again. For UI we want under 200ms p95 — do we have a config that hits that and still gives decent economy?
[07:53] Anya: For UI: conservative batch+cache with int8 disabled for UI routes gives p95 ~180ms and tokens/sec/$ slightly lower (-12% from the aggressive). For background tasks you can be aggressive and save ~35%. So route-level policy is recommended.
[08:11] James: One more operational ask: can Redwood surface per-route cost anomalies? We had a spike last week where a training job accidentally pointed at the live endpoint and cost spiked.
[08:21] Anya: Console already has per-route cost alerts and anomaly detection — we can preconfigure alerts for you and one of our support engineers can help tune thresholds.
[08:29] Samir: We're also proposing a runbook — if cost > X% day-over-day trigger a scale-down and alert. We'll share a draft.
[08:36] Marta: Good.
[08:37] Priya: For the microbench, how long will Redwood need to run to collect meaningful p95 stats?
[08:42] Anya: For steady-state, 30-60 minutes at production concurrency is usually enough to get stable p95 and tokens/sec numbers. For long-tail quality evals run overnight for 100k tokens.
[08:56] James: We'll do the 100k overnight and post results.
[08:59] Anya: Great. I'll note that in action items.
[09:02] Samir: Any blockers on the pilot extension? Marta?
[09:06] Marta: Finance needs the reserved forecast to sign; also legal asked for updated SOC 2 scope.
[09:12] Samir: We'll attach updated SOC 2 + compliance page and the forecast.
[09:16] Marta: Thanks.
[09:17] Priya: Quick nit — when you mention tokens/sec/$ can you include a column that shows effective per-request cost for our top 10 routes? That would help product prioritize.
[09:25] Anya: Yes, the per-route export will include per-request median and p95 cost columns. I'll put that in the sheet.
[09:31] James: On the KV cache TTL test — can you give us an estimate of memory overhead? We don't want to blow out node memory.
[09:36] Anya: With 1.5GB per instance cap we saw ~8% memory pressure on pilot nodes. Increasing TTL to 30m bumped it to ~11%. It's linear with session count; we'll give you a pro forma estimate for your observed active sessions.
[09:51] Marta: Ok, so to recap — Redwood will share: updated batching + cache config, per-route CSV, SOC2 scope, and a forecast for reserved hours. LumenWorks will run overnight 100k token benchmark and surface traces. Microbench next week to try TTL=30m cache test. Action items assigned.
[10:14] Samir: Yep. Anything else?
[10:18] James: One question — is there a way to flag high-cost requests in real-time and auto-throttle?
[10:23] Anya: Yes, you can set per-route caps and auto-throttle or route to cheaper variant; Redwood has policing rules in the routing layer. We'll share a template.
[10:33] Marta: Great — thanks everyone.
[10:35] Priya: Thanks.
[10:37] Samir: Thanks, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and schedule the microbench.
[10:41] Anya: Bye all.
[10:42] [END]
